analysis.one_liner: Orders the FTC to study whether oil and gas companies are inflating pump prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one cosponsor, the bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee for two years without a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether oil and gas companies engaged in anti-competitive or collusive conduct that raised prices for consumers, including whether companies spent money on stock buybacks instead of producing more fuel. The FTC would have had to report its findings to Congress annually for three years, with recommendations for fixing any problems it found. It came with $15 million a year in funding and up to 50 new FTC staff to do the work.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay gas prices would benefit from an official, public investigation into whether oil companies' conduct — collusion, price gouging, or stock buybacks that shrink fuel supply — inflated costs at the pump, and from the FTC's recommendations for follow-up action [S2][S3]. State attorneys general would gain a federal partner in looking into the same conduct [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers paying prices at the pump

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FTC, working with state attorneys general where appropriate, to study anti-competitive, collusive, or other conduct in oil and gas markets, including the actual price consumers pay.

Specifically directs the study to examine whether oil companies inflated consumer costs or engaged in price gouging, delayed producing or delivering more fuel, and whether they spent money on stock buybacks or cut production investment instead of expanding fuel supply.
Also examines whether company conduct restricted the availability or affordability of alternative fuels or vehicle technology.
Requires annual reports to Congress for three years with recommendations for legislation or administrative action to create fair, competitive, and transparent gas markets.
Provides real capacity to do the work: up to 50 additional FTC hires and $15 million in funding for each of fiscal years 2024 and 2025.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would bear the cost of federal scrutiny of their pricing, buybacks, and supply decisions, which could lead to enforcement or legislation restricting their conduct [S3]. Taxpayers would fund the study — $15 million a year for two fiscal years, plus 50 new FTC positions [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; taxpayers fund the study

drawbacks.text: The bill is a study, not relief: it would not lower a single pump price on its own, and its only concrete output is reports with non-binding recommendations to Congress.
It costs taxpayers $30 million over two years and up to 50 new FTC hires to produce those reports, at a time when the FTC already has legal authority to investigate oil markets on its own.
There is no guarantee the findings would lead to any action — Congress would still have to pass whatever legislation the FTC recommends, which the bill cannot compel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is small and the potential value is real but indirect: an official finding that oil companies' conduct raised pump prices could support enforcement or future legislation, which matters to households that feel gas prices directly. But the bill's design is deliberately cautious — three years of reports and recommendations rather than any direct cap, enforcement, or price relief — so even full success would only set the stage for action rather than deliver it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cortez Masto introduced the bill on January 25, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The committee took no further action for the entire two-year Congress — no hearing, no markup, and no vote ever appears in the bill's action history.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, Senator Ben Ray Luján, over its lifetime.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the measure still stuck in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies came out ahead: the study of their pricing, stock buybacks, and supply decisions that Congress might have mandated never happened, and no scrutiny or follow-up legislation resulted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies, avoiding FTC scrutiny

for.name: Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 1 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Senator Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico cosponsored the bill; he was its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place; the bill had two Democratic senators behind it and the Senate never considered it, so no partisan split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have forced a federal investigation into whether these companies colluded, gouged prices, or prioritized stock buybacks over fuel supply — conduct that shows up in what consumers pay at the pump. Avoiding that scrutiny protects their pricing and capital-allocation decisions.

The study was directed to examine whether oil company conduct restricted the availability or affordability of alternative fuels and vehicle technology, so any findings would support these competitors.
The bill would have expanded the FTC's oil-and-gas docket with 50 new hires and $15 million a year, and required it to publish findings that could anchor future enforcement or legislation.
